mcq.q: Amit lends his car free of charge to his friend Bala for a week's holiday. This is:
options: A bailment for reward
A pledge
A gratuitous bailment for the sole benefit of the bailee
Not a bailment, as no money is involved
mcq.explain: Delivery of a car for a purpose, to be returned afterwards, is a bailment under Section 148 even without payment. Since Amit charges nothing and only Bala benefits, it is a gratuitous bailment for the exclusive benefit of the bailee. There is no debt being secured, so it is not a pledge.
mcq.fast: No payment = gratuitous; who benefits? Only the borrower -> "for the benefit of the bailee".

mcq.q: Under Section 151, in all cases of bailment the bailee must take the care of the goods that:
options: An expert insurer would take
He takes of his own goods, however careless he is
A reasonably prudent person would give to his own similar goods
The bailor specifically demands
mcq.explain: Section 151 sets the standard: the care a reasonably prudent person would give to his own goods of similar quantity, quality and value in similar circumstances. Section 152 then frees him from liability for loss if he took that care, unless a special contract says otherwise.
mcq.fast: Standard = ordinary prudent man with his own similar goods.

mcq.q: In a bailment for reward, the bailor did not know of a defect in the goods that caused injury to the bailee. The bailor is:
options: Liable, whether or not he was aware of the defect — Section 150
Not liable, since he was unaware
Liable only if the bailment was gratuitous
Liable only for half the damage
mcq.explain: Section 150 requires the bailor to disclose known faults. For bailments for hire, it adds that the bailor is responsible for damage arising from faults in the goods whether or not he was aware of their existence. In a gratuitous bailment he is liable only for faults he knew of and did not disclose.
mcq.fast: Hire = liable even if unaware. Gratuitous = only known faults.

mcq.q: A finder of lost goods may sell them when the owner cannot be found with reasonable diligence and the lawful charges of the finder amount to:
options: One-half of their value
Two-thirds of the value of the goods — Section 169
One-third of their value
The full value of the goods
mcq.explain: Section 169 permits the finder to sell if the thing is commonly the subject of sale, cannot be traced to its owner with reasonable diligence (or the owner refuses to pay lawful charges), and either it is likely to perish or lose most of its value, or the finder's lawful charges reach two-thirds of its value.
mcq.fast: Finder's sale trigger: perishing, or charges reach 2/3 of value.

mcq.q: Which of these persons has a GENERAL lien under Section 171?
options: A tailor who stitched a suit
A goldsmith who made a ring
A carpenter who repaired a chair
Bankers
mcq.explain: Section 171 gives a general lien — a right to retain any goods of the customer for a general balance of account — to bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers. Tailors, goldsmiths and carpenters have only a particular lien under Section 170 over the specific goods on which they worked.
mcq.topic: Right of lien — particular and general (Sections 170, 171)
mcq.fast: General lien list = Bankers, Factors, Wharfingers, Attorneys, Policy-brokers ("BFWAP").

mcq.q: On the pawnor's default, the pawnee sells the pledged goods after reasonable notice. The sale yields ₹70,000 against a debt of ₹85,000. The pawnor:
options: Is fully discharged
Remains liable to pay the balance of ₹15,000 — Section 176
Can claim ₹15,000 from the pawnee
Can set aside the sale
mcq.explain: Section 176 gives the pawnee, on default, the right to sue or to sell after reasonable notice. If the proceeds are less than the amount due, the pawnor remains liable to pay the balance; if they are more, the pawnee must pay the surplus to the pawnor. Here ₹85,000 − ₹70,000 = ₹15,000 is still due.
mcq.fast: Pledge sale: shortfall -> pawnor pays; surplus -> pawnee returns.

mcq.q: Which is a key difference between bailment and pledge?
options: In a pledge, ownership passes to the pawnee
A pledge can only be of immovable property
A bailee can always sell the goods on default
A pledge is a bailment whose purpose is to secure a debt or a promise
mcq.explain: Section 172: a pledge is a bailment made to secure a debt or the performance of a promise. Ownership never passes in either case. A pawnee has a statutory right of sale on default (Section 176), but an ordinary bailee has no such right. Both relate only to movable goods.
mcq.topic: Pledge by non-owners and bailment vs pledge
mcq.fast: Pledge = bailment + security purpose. Ownership never passes in either.
